title: Backup and DR in Plain English: Protect, Restore, Recover
summary: Separate backup, replication, recovery objectives and disaster recovery so protection design matches business impact.
plain_language_explanation: Backups create recoverable copies. Replication keeps another copy of live data or workloads. Disaster recovery is the wider plan for restoring business service after a major outage. RPO defines acceptable data loss; RTO defines acceptable recovery time. A green backup job does not prove the service is recoverable.
quick_check: Why can a successful backup job still fail the business recovery requirement?

title: RPO, RTO, Dependency Mapping and Protection Scope
summary: Turn business recovery objectives into workload, data and dependency protection requirements.
objective: Translate business impact, RPO/RTO and dependency maps into explicit protection and recovery requirements.
body_outline: Classify services by business impact rather than giving every workload the same protection tier.
Define RPO and RTO per service and prove that backup frequency, replication and restore process can meet them.
Map identity, DNS, certificates, secrets, networks, databases, storage, monitoring and external dependencies.
Treat configuration, metadata and encryption-key recovery as part of the recovery scope.
Identify recovery order and minimum viable service state before a disaster occurs.
Document ownership for declaring disaster, initiating restore, validating service and returning to normal operations.

title: Backup Integrity, Immutability and Restore Assurance
summary: Design protection so recovery copies are trustworthy, isolated from common failure modes and routinely proven by restore testing.
objective: Explain why recoverability depends on protected copies, retention controls, key access, integrity checks and tested restores.
body_outline: Separate control-plane compromise from backup-data compromise when designing administrative boundaries.
Use immutable or locked retention controls where the service and compliance model support them.
Protect backup credentials, encryption keys and vault access with least privilege and separation of duties.
Monitor backup failures, skipped resources, retention drift and policy coverage gaps.
Perform restore validation in an isolated or approved test location instead of assuming job success equals recoverability.
Record restore duration, data consistency, dependency gaps and evidence against RPO/RTO targets.

title: Disaster Recovery Orchestration, Failover and Failback
summary: Connect backup, replication, runbooks, recovery sequencing, validation and failback into a controlled disaster recovery operating model.
architecture_notes: A DR plan coordinates people, authority, data protection, replication, dependencies, recovery sequencing, validation and failback. Replication can shorten recovery time but can also replicate corruption or malicious changes. Backup provides historical recovery points. Mature designs use both where justified, with rehearsed runbooks and evidence that failover and failback protect data consistency.
failure_modes: backup exists but required identity or DNS dependencies are missing
replication is healthy but the replica contains the same logical corruption
recovery plan restores compute before network, secrets or databases are ready
test failover is never performed because production failover is considered too risky
failover succeeds but business validation and monitoring are absent
failback starts before resynchronization and change ownership are understood
ransomware compromises both production and mutable backup administration
enterprise_design_notes: Define declaration authority, recovery tiers, isolated restore testing, immutable copies where appropriate, cross-region/site dependencies, communication paths, business validation, and a separate failback plan.

title: Read-Only Recoverability Evidence Pack
summary: Collect protection, recovery-point and DR configuration evidence without running restores, failovers or retention changes.
objective: Produce a timestamped recoverability inventory before any restore, failover or policy change is proposed.
steps: Record the approved workload, business owner, RPO, RTO and recovery tier.
Inventory configured backup policies, protected items and recent recovery-point metadata without changing retention.
Record immutable/locked retention settings where visible without altering them.
Inventory replication or DR-plan metadata and current health without initiating test or production failover.
Record key dependencies, latest successful restore-test evidence and unresolved protection gaps.
Classify findings as coverage, integrity, retention, dependency, replication, orchestration or validation gaps.
expected_result: A read-only recovery evidence pack showing protection scope, recovery-point metadata, policy state and DR dependencies without mutation.
rollback: Not required; prescribed activities are inventory-only.

title: Backup Failure, Restore Failure or DR Incident Decision Tree
summary: Separate protection, integrity, dependency, authorization, replication and orchestration failures before changing recovery controls.
diagnostic_order: Confirm workload, scope, recovery objective and incident time window.
Determine whether the issue is backup creation, recovery-point availability, integrity, authorization, key access, dependency readiness, replication health or orchestration.
Preserve job, policy and recovery-point evidence before retrying or deleting anything.
For restore failures, validate target capacity, network, identity, key, storage and application dependencies separately.
For DR incidents, verify replication state, recovery sequence, DNS/network cutover and business validation before failover or failback.
Escalate when remediation requires retention changes, vault deletion, backup-policy mutation, restore into production, failover, failback, key changes or destructive cleanup.
escalation_boundary: Do not delete recovery points, lower retention, disable immutability, change encryption keys, restore into production, initiate failover/failback or overwrite source data without explicit recovery/change authority.

title: Backup and Disaster Recovery Foundations Assessment
summary: Scenario assessment covering RPO/RTO, immutability, restore testing, replication and DR governance.

assessment_items.question: What is the difference between RPO and RTO?
assessment_items.answer: RPO is the acceptable amount of data loss measured in time; RTO is the acceptable time to restore service.

assessment_items.question: Why is replication not a replacement for backup?
assessment_items.answer: Replication can copy corruption, deletion or malicious changes. Backup provides historical recovery points that can support rollback to an earlier state.

assessment_items.question: What does immutability protect against?
assessment_items.answer: It limits deletion or modification of protected recovery data during the retention period, reducing risk from administrative compromise or ransomware.

assessment_items.question: What proves recoverability better than a successful backup job?
assessment_items.answer: A documented restore test that verifies data, dependencies, application consistency, recovery time and business validation against the required objectives.
